title: iPadOS Settings Menu Simulator - Browse All 35 Panels
h1: Walk the iPad Settings tree without touching a tablet
desc: Explore the iPadOS Settings layout in a free browser simulator: 35 top-level panels, ten levels deep, with sample device values clearly marked as samples.
lede: Tablet settings look simple until you need something specific, and then the list keeps going. This tablet layout carries more than sixteen hundred rows spread across ten levels of nesting, which is a lot of tapping to do on borrowed hardware. Running the same tree in a browser lets you look before you touch anything real.
character: The first thing you notice is that the top level is a long single column rather than a set of categories. Airplane Mode, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Cellular Data sit at the very top, then attention controls like Notifications, Sounds, Focus and Screen Time, then the hardware group of Battery, General, Control Center and Display & Brightness. After that come Home Screen & Multitasking, Accessibility and Wallpaper, and only then the per-app rows for Safari, Contacts, Calendar, Notes and the rest. The ordering is a rough priority list rather than a taxonomy, and it rewards people who remember positions rather than names.

Depth is where this layout differs from its phone sibling. Ten levels is unusual, and the extra rungs mostly live under General, Accessibility and Privacy & Security, where a single toggle can sit four or five taps below the surface. Grouping is inconsistent by design: Apple Pencil gets its own top-level row because the hardware is optional, while Face ID & Passcode carries both biometrics and the passcode policy. Newcomers usually get lost between Home Screen & Multitasking and Display & Brightness, because both sound like they own the screen and neither owns all of it.
history: The layout inherits its shape from the iPhone, where a flat scrolling list of panels made sense on a small screen, and it has been stretched rather than redrawn as the tablet gained multitasking, an optional stylus and cellular hardware. Splitting the tablet line into its own named release made room for tablet-specific rows. The versions offered here, 17.5, 17.0 and 16.6, sit close together in time and are useful mainly for spotting where a panel was renamed, moved up the list, or gained a new sub-screen.

notable.why: This decides whether a focus mode you switch on here also silences your other Apple hardware. People turn on a work mode on the tablet and then wonder why the phone went quiet too, and this single row is the reason.

notable.path: Settings > Wi-Fi > Ask to Join Networks
notable.why: It controls how aggressively the tablet offers unknown networks when nothing known is in range. Set it one way and you get constant prompts in a cafe, set it the other and you sit offline wondering why nothing connected.

Rather than muting apps one by one, this batches non-urgent alerts and delivers them at times you choose. It is the closest thing to a quiet inbox for notifications, and most people never find it because it sits above the app list.

audience: Helpdesk staff who talk tablet owners through a fix by phone benefit most, because they can read the exact row order aloud instead of guessing. Teachers preparing a lesson on device privacy can rehearse the click path before class. Parents setting up a first tablet can see what Screen Time actually asks for. And anyone weighing a tablet purchase can judge how much of the interface they would have to learn.

faq.q: Is this the real iPadOS settings layout?
faq.a: The menu names, their order and their nesting mirror the shipping interface, reconstructed panel by panel rather than pulled from published source, since this system is not open source. Device details such as network names, storage figures and build numbers are sample values shown for realism and are labelled that way.

faq.q: Can I compare 17.5 with 16.6 side by side?
faq.a: Yes. Switch versions from the picker and the tree reloads at the same position where possible, so you can see whether a row moved, gained a sub-screen or changed wording. Comparison mode also puts two different systems next to each other if you want a cross-platform view.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything or sign in?
faq.a: No. Everything runs in the browser with no account, no download and no connection to a real device. Nothing you tap changes any hardware, which is why it works for practising a support script or testing a click path you plan to send to somebody else.

title: ChromeOS Settings Simulator: Chromebook Menu Explorer
h1: See how a Chromebook sorts its twelve settings groups
desc: Browse the ChromeOS settings tree in a free offline simulator: twelve grouped sections, 618 rows, five levels deep, with sample values marked as samples.
lede: Twelve headings and just over six hundred rows is a tight budget for a full desktop system, and the tidiness is deliberate. Where other laptop systems scatter controls across dozens of panels, this one leans on a small set of named groups and a search box. Clicking through the whole thing in a browser takes minutes rather than an afternoon.
character: The organising idea is grouping by question rather than by component. Network, Bluetooth and Connected devices answer what am I talking to. Accounts and Kerberos answer who am I. Device gathers everything physical, from Mouse and Touchpad through Keyboard and inputs to Display, Audio, Print and Scan. Wallpaper and style, Privacy and security, Apps and Accessibility each own a clear domain, and System preferences catches the leftovers before About ChromeOS closes the list. Nothing sits at the top level unless it names a category, which is why twelve entries can cover so much ground.

Five levels is shallow for a desktop system, and that shallowness is the trade. You reach almost anything in three clicks, but the middle screens get crowded, and Device in particular is a long scroll rather than a menu. Compared with a traditional laptop control panel, where each device class gets its own icon, this collapses them into one page and relies on headings to break it up. Newcomers most often stall on Connected devices, which sounds like Bluetooth but actually handles phone pairing and Nearby Share, and on System preferences, whose name promises more than it holds.
history: Settings here began as a page inside the browser, which is why it still behaves like a document with sections rather than a stack of separate windows. As the system grew beyond the browser to handle styluses, Android apps, printers and phone pairing, the page was reorganised into named groups instead of gaining new top-level rows. Because the platform is open source, the titles and nesting can be taken from the source itself. The two builds offered here, 124 and 120, are close neighbours and mostly show wording and regrouping changes.

notable.why: Scroll direction, tap-to-click and sensitivity all live here, and they are the first things people change on a borrowed machine. Knowing the row sits under Device rather than under a pointing-device panel saves a genuinely annoying hunt.

This is the list the machine reconnects to automatically. When a laptop keeps rejoining a slow guest network instead of the good one, this screen is where you remove the bad entry rather than fighting it at the connection prompt.

It governs who can send you files without pairing and how visible you are while idle. Worth finding because the default visibility setting surprises people in offices and classrooms where many machines sit within range.

audience: School IT staff who manage carts of identical laptops get the most out of this, since they can rehearse a rollout path and screenshot it for a handout without unboxing anything. Support agents can confirm whether a control lives under Device or System preferences before they say it aloud. Anyone moving from a Windows or Mac laptop can see how much smaller the settings surface really is before committing to the switch.

faq.q: Does this match a real Chromebook exactly?
faq.a: The menu titles, their order and their nesting come from the open source project, so the structure matches. What cannot match is device state: network names, connected accessories and hardware details are sample values chosen to make the screens readable, and the simulator marks them as samples rather than presenting them as yours.

faq.q: Why are there only twelve top-level entries?
faq.a: The design groups by purpose instead of by component, so a single Device entry covers pointing devices, keyboard, display, audio and printing. Fewer headings mean longer pages, and the built-in search on real hardware is meant to carry the load when you already know the name of what you want.

faq.q: Can I use this to write instructions for other people?
faq.a: Yes. The step recorder captures the exact click path you take through the tree so it can be replayed or shared, which is quicker than writing out each turn by hand. There is also an embeddable widget if you want the tree to sit inside your own help page.

title: CarPlay Settings Simulator - Every In-Car Menu Panel
h1: Tap through the in-car settings screen while parked
desc: Try the CarPlay settings layout in a free browser simulator: twelve panels, 81 rows, three levels deep, on a car dashboard frame with sample values marked.
lede: Dashboard interfaces are built to be forgotten. You get twelve panels, eighty-one rows and never more than three levels, because anything deeper would be dangerous to operate while moving. That restraint makes the whole tree small enough to learn in one sitting, which is exactly the sort of thing worth doing before you are behind the wheel.
character: Every entry earns its place by being something you would want changed once and then left alone. Wallpaper and Appearance handle how the screen looks at night. App Layout is a grid editor for the home screen, listing Maps, Phone, Music, Messages, Now Playing, Podcasts, Calendar, Audiobooks, Settings and Spotify. Do Not Disturb While Driving, Driving Focus and Announce Messages with Siri all concern interruption. Siri Suggestions, Suggested Apps and Sound cover what the system offers unprompted. Allow CarPlay While Locked and Manage Cars are the pairing and security pair. There is no catch-all panel at all.

Three levels is the whole point of comparison with the phone this connects to. The phone version of the same brand piles ten levels of nesting into thirty-five panels; here the same designers stripped it back to a list you can read at a glance. Related items are duplicated rather than nested, which is why Announce Messages with Siri appears both as a top-level row and inside Sound. That repetition looks untidy on a page but works in a car, where you should not have to remember which branch you took. Confusion usually comes from Appearance and Wallpaper sounding interchangeable.
history: The in-car layout started as a mirror of the phone screen with almost nothing configurable, and controls were added only when drivers had no other way to reach them, which is why the panel count stayed small. Grid arrangement, night appearance and interruption handling arrived as separate additions rather than as one redesign. The two versions offered here, 17.5 and 16.6, sit a generation apart and are useful for seeing which rows are recent and which have been there since the interface settled into its current shape.

notable.why: The grid editor decides what greets you when the engine starts. Moving Now Playing to the first page means audio controls are one glance away instead of one hunt away, which matters more than any other choice on this screen.

notable.path: Settings > Sound > Announce Messages with Siri
notable.why: This turns incoming messages into spoken text so you never look down at the display. It is the single row that changes driving behaviour most, and it also appears at the top level because of how often people go looking for it.

Adds the posted limit to the navigation view alongside your route. Drivers in unfamiliar regions find it useful, and it sits beside Show Compass in a panel most people never open because they assume map options live in the map app.

audience: Car dealership staff running a handover benefit directly, since they can show the screen on a laptop rather than reaching across a passenger seat. Rental agents explaining pairing to a customer get the same advantage. Drivers who have just bought a used vehicle can find out what the head unit will offer before the first trip, and accessibility trainers can demonstrate the announcement and focus controls without anyone needing to start an engine.

faq.q: Where do these CarPlay settings actually live on a real car?
faq.a: Most of them appear on the dashboard screen itself once a phone is connected, and some mirror controls that also exist on the phone. The simulator reproduces the dashboard arrangement, reconstructed from the shipping interface rather than from published source, since this system is not open source.

faq.q: Why are there so few settings compared with a phone?
faq.a: Anything that takes more than a glance is a hazard while driving, so the design keeps the tree three levels deep and repeats important rows instead of burying them. Configuration that can wait is left on the phone, which is why the in-car list holds eighty-one rows rather than thousands.

faq.q: Can I see the difference between the two versions?
faq.a: Yes. Switch between 17.5 and 16.6 in the picker to see which panels existed in each and how the wording changed. Because the tree is small, a side-by-side pass takes only a few minutes and makes generational changes much easier to spot than on a larger system.

title: Mac OS X Preferences Simulator: Snow Leopard Panels
h1: Revisit the System Preferences grid of Snow Leopard
desc: Open the Mac OS X System Preferences layout in a free browser simulator: 25 panes, 194 rows, three levels deep, with sample values marked as samples.
lede: Before settings became an endless scrolling list, they were a grid of little icons in a single window, and you learned the picture rather than the words. Twenty-five panes, one hundred and ninety-four rows and never more than three levels means the whole system fits on one screen. Opening that window again in a browser is oddly clarifying.
character: The grid arranges panes by rough theme rather than alphabetically, and the themes are visible at a glance. Appearance, Desktop & Screen Saver, Dock, Exposé & Spaces and Language & Text form the personal row. Displays, Network, Sound, Keyboard, Trackpad, Mouse, Print & Fax, Bluetooth and CDs & DVDs make up the hardware block. Accounts, Date & Time, Software Update, Universal Access, Security, Energy Saver, Sharing, Spotlight, Startup Disk, Time Machine and Speech cover the system itself. Each pane is a self-contained window with its own controls, so the design has no shared navigation to learn.

What makes this feel different from a modern settings app is that depth is capped by the window. Three levels is all a pane can hold before it needs a sheet or a separate tab, so options are laid out across the surface instead of stacked below it. Exposé & Spaces packs corner triggers, keyboard shortcuts and virtual desktops into one dense pane. Language & Text mixes region lists with text substitution. Newcomers coming back to it now trip over the split between Security, Accounts and Sharing, three panes that each hold a piece of what a single privacy screen would cover today.
history: System Preferences replaced the older stack of separate control files with one window holding a grid of panes, and each release added panes as new hardware and services arrived rather than reorganising what was there. Spaces, Time Machine and Spotlight all show up as their own icons for that reason. The two versions offered here, 10.6 and 10.5, sit either side of a large under-the-hood rewrite that changed relatively little at the surface, so comparing them is mostly an exercise in spotting removed and renamed panes.

notable.why: This is the switch that turns one desktop into several. Virtual desktops were unfamiliar then and are standard now, so seeing the original opt-in framing explains why the feature still behaves the way it does on later machines.

Choosing between the two minimise animations was the classic first tweak on a new machine. It does nothing functional, which is precisely why it survives in memory as the thing everyone changed within five minutes of opening the box.

notable.path: Settings > Appearance > Show scroll bars automatically
notable.why: Deciding when scroll bars appear looks trivial until a bar vanishes and you cannot tell how long a document is. This row sits in the pane where colour themes live, which is where most people forget to look.

audience: People maintaining older studio or lab machines still running this generation get practical use, since they can locate a pane before walking to the hardware. Interface students comparing a grid of panes with a modern scrolling list have both open at once. Writers and video makers working on period-accurate scenes can check what a pane actually held, and anyone restoring an old machine can plan the setup order before booting it.

faq.q: Is this the real Snow Leopard System Preferences?
faq.a: The pane names, their grouping and their contents follow the shipping interface, reconstructed screen by screen rather than taken from published source, because this system is not open source. Anything that would belong to a specific machine, such as display resolutions in use or account names, appears as clearly marked sample values.

faq.q: What is the difference between 10.6 and 10.5 here?
faq.a: Mostly panes appearing, disappearing or being renamed, plus small changes inside individual panes. Switch between the two in the picker and the tree reloads so you can look at the same pane in both. The larger differences between those releases were internal and never surfaced in the preferences window.

faq.q: Why does it look so different from a current Mac?
faq.a: Preferences were a grid of independent panes rather than one continuous list with a sidebar, and each pane opened as its own screen. The later redesign folded those panes into a single scrolling column borrowed from the phone interface, which is the main reason old click paths no longer match new ones.

title: Zepp OS Settings Simulator for Amazfit Smartwatches
h1: Turn a watch dial into ten readable settings screens
desc: Explore the Zepp OS watch settings menu in a free browser simulator: ten sections, 78 rows, three levels deep, shown on a watch frame with sample values.
lede: Reading a settings menu on a screen the size of a postage stamp is a chore, and scrolling it with a fingertip is worse. Ten sections and seventy-eight rows is a small tree by any measure, but on a wrist it still means a lot of swiping. Seeing the whole thing laid out flat removes the guesswork.
character: The sections read like a list of jobs the watch actually does. Connection gathers Phone, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, Airplane Mode, Alexa and Find my phone, so everything involving another device sits in one place. Watch Faces handles appearance and the always-on behaviour. Display, Sound and Vibration cover output. Health Monitoring is the section that justifies the hardware, holding heart rate, sleep, stress and blood oxygen tracking. Notifications, Workouts, Battery, System and About finish the list. Nothing is nested for the sake of tidiness, because a hidden row on a watch is effectively a missing row.

Three levels is the ceiling, and most useful controls sit at two. The real design tension shows up in Health Monitoring, where each sensor has its own frequency and threshold options that quietly govern how long the battery lasts. Turning on continuous heart rate and blood oxygen changes the charging routine more than anything in the Battery section does, but the two are not connected in the menu. That split is where newcomers get caught: they look for power settings under Battery and never realise the sensors are the thing draining it.
history: Watch settings here grew out of a companion-phone model, where the phone app held most configuration and the wrist showed only what you might change while wearing it. Over time more moved onto the watch itself, particularly around health sensors and notification handling, which is why those sections carry the most rows. The two versions listed, Zepp OS 4 and Zepp OS 3, represent a shift toward doing more on device, so comparing them shows sections gaining depth rather than the top-level list changing shape.

notable.why: Blood oxygen measurement is the most battery-hungry sensor option on the watch. Whether it samples continuously or only when asked is decided here, and it explains most complaints about a watch that suddenly stopped lasting a week.

notable.path: Settings > Watch Faces > Always On Display
notable.why: Keeping the dial lit means you can read the time without moving your arm, at a real cost in runtime. It sits under faces rather than under display, which is why people hunt for it in the wrong section.

notable.path: Settings > Display > Raise wrist to wake
notable.why: The gesture that lights the screen when you turn your arm sounds trivial until it fires all night or fails during a workout. Adjusting it is the difference between a watch that feels responsive and one that feels broken.

audience: Retail staff demonstrating a watch on a busy counter can show the menu on a larger screen instead of holding a tiny dial up to a customer. Runners deciding which tracking to leave on before a long event can plan the whole configuration in advance. Older wearers or anyone helping a relative set one up can rehearse the taps, and reviewers comparing wearables can see what a section actually contains.

faq.q: Does this work for all Amazfit watches?
faq.a: The structure follows the platform rather than a single model, so section names and their order match across watches running the same generation. Individual hardware differences mean a model without a particular sensor will not show that row. Sensor readings and battery figures here are sample values, not measurements from anything real.

faq.q: How was this layout put together?
faq.a: It is reconstructed from the shipping interface rather than extracted from published source, since the platform is not open source. That means the names and their arrangement follow what the watch displays. Device-specific details such as a paired phone name or a battery percentage are sample values shown so the screens read naturally.

faq.q: Can I check settings before buying a watch?
faq.a: That is one of the more common uses. Walking Health Monitoring and Notifications tells you what the watch can track and how much control you get over alerts, which is usually more informative than a specification list. You can also put it beside another wearable using comparison mode.

title: Roku OS Settings Simulator: TV Menus in Your Browser
h1: Practise the television settings menu before you sit down
desc: Step through the Roku OS settings menu in a free browser simulator: eight sections, 91 rows, three levels deep, on a TV frame with marked sample values.
lede: Television menus are driven with a directional pad from across a room, which changes everything about how they can be built. Eight sections, ninety-one rows and three levels is about as much as anyone can navigate with five buttons and no pointer. Working through that structure with a mouse first makes the remote far less frustrating later.
character: Constraint shapes this layout more than philosophy does. Network, Display type, Audio, Theme, TV picture settings, Remotes and devices, System and Account is the entire top level, and each one maps to a physical concern you might have while sitting in front of the set. Display type deals with resolution and refresh rate. Audio covers output formats including Dolby and passthrough options plus volume levelling. Theme holds screensavers and visual styles. TV picture settings carries the picture presets. Nothing abstract appears at the top level, because a name you have to think about costs several button presses to recover from.

The unusual part is that picture and display are deliberately separated. Display type is about the signal the box sends, while TV picture settings is about how the panel renders it, and the two live in different sections despite feeling like one topic to most viewers. Audio splits the same way, with output format in one place and loudness behaviour in another. Compared with a smart television built by a panel manufacturer, where everything hides behind a single picture menu, this separation is more honest but harder to guess. That is where remote-in-hand confusion usually starts.
history: The menu began on a small streaming box with no tuner and no picture controls, so early versions needed little more than network, display output and account. As the software moved onto televisions themselves, sections for picture presets and remote pairing were added alongside the originals rather than folded into them, which explains the split between signal and panel settings. The two versions offered here, Roku OS 14 and Roku OS 13, are close together and mostly show sections gaining rows as audio and screensaver options expanded.

notable.why: This evens out the jump between quiet dialogue and loud advertising. It is the single change most likely to stop late-night viewers reaching for the remote every few minutes, and it sits below the format options that people usually stop reading at.

It stops playback after a period without input, which saves data on a metered connection and prevents a stream running all night. Useful in shared houses and holiday rentals where nobody notices the television has been playing for hours.

Idle screens run for a long time on a television, so what fills them matters more than it sounds. Choosing your own instead of the default is a small change that makes a shared living room feel less like a shop display.

audience: Hotel and rental hosts configuring many identical sets benefit most, because they can write the button sequence once and hand it to staff. Support agents talking a caller through picture problems can confirm whether an option lives under Display type or TV picture settings before they guess. Anyone setting up a television for a relative who struggles with remotes can prepare the whole path, then read it out step by step over the phone.

faq.q: Is this the same menu as on my television?
faq.a: The section names and their arrangement follow the shipping interface, reconstructed screen by screen because the platform is not open source. Televisions from different manufacturers can expose slightly different picture options depending on the panel. Anything specific to a set, such as detected resolution or paired remotes, appears here as a sample value.

faq.q: Why are picture and display settings in separate places?
faq.a: Display type controls the signal format the software sends out, while TV picture settings controls how the panel processes what it receives. The split reflects how the software grew from a streaming box that had no panel of its own, and it survives on televisions where both roles now sit in one device.

faq.q: Can I search for a setting instead of browsing?
faq.a: Yes. The simulator has a search that finds which system holds a given setting and where it sits, which helps when you know what you want to change but not what the menu calls it. On a television that saves a genuinely tedious amount of pressing arrow keys.

title: Firefox OS Settings Simulator: Gaia Menus Preserved
h1: Look inside the settings app of a discontinued phone
desc: Browse the Firefox OS settings tree in a free browser simulator: 39 sections, 365 rows, three levels deep, built from Gaia source with sample values marked.
lede: Discontinued platforms tend to vanish along with the hardware, and their interfaces survive only in screenshots. This one is different, because the settings app was open source and the whole tree can still be read from it. Thirty-nine sections and three hundred and sixty-five rows is a complete phone, preserved rather than remembered.
character: The top level is long and unapologetically flat. Airplane Mode, Geolocation and Wi-Fi come first, then a solid block of telephony with SIM Manager, Call Settings, Messaging Settings and Cellular & Data, followed by Bluetooth, NFC and Internet Sharing. Sound, Display, Home Screens, Search, Navigation and Notifications handle the interface. Then come Date & Time, Language, Keyboards, Themes and Add-ons, and a security run of Firefox Accounts, Find My Device, Screen Lock, SIM Security, App Permissions, Do Not Track and Browsing Privacy. Storage is split three ways, and Developer sits in the open near the end.

Two things stand out against phones sold today. First, the browser vocabulary leaks everywhere: Do Not Track and Browsing Privacy are top-level phone settings here, not options buried in a browser, because the whole system was the browser. Second, telephony gets four separate sections where a modern phone gives it one, and dual-SIM handling is treated as normal rather than as an edge case. Depth stays at three levels throughout, so the list is long but never deep. Newcomers get lost among USB Storage, Media Storage and Application Storage, three sections whose names describe implementation rather than what you actually want to clear.
history: The settings app was part of Gaia, the interface layer written in web technologies, which is why its structure can be read directly from source rather than reconstructed from screenshots. Sections were added as the platform reached new markets, particularly around dual-SIM handling and low-cost hardware, and the browser-derived privacy controls were present from early on. The two versions offered here, 2.5 and 2.2, come from the final stretch of the project, so the differences between them are small refinements rather than the larger reorganisations of earlier years.

notable.path: Settings > Call Settings > Fixed Dialing Numbers
notable.why: This restricts outgoing calls to an approved list stored on the SIM. It was standard on feature phones and has largely disappeared from modern menus, so it is a good example of a control that ordinary users once expected to find.

Deciding whether wireless stays awake with the screen off was a real battery choice on hardware this modest. Modern phones make the decision for you, which is exactly why seeing it offered as a user setting is interesting.

Asking the network to confirm a message arrived was a normal expectation of text messaging. Finding it here, beside read reports and roaming behaviour, shows how much messaging configuration once lived in the operating system rather than in an app.

audience: Interface researchers and students studying how mobile platforms diverged get concrete material rather than recollection. Developers who worked on web-based platforms can check what shipped against what they remember. Collectors running the hardware, and anyone writing about the period, can confirm a menu path instead of guessing at it. Teachers covering the history of mobile operating systems can show a full working tree during a lesson.

faq.q: Can I still use Firefox OS on a phone?
faq.a: The platform was discontinued and no current handset ships with it, so this is a record rather than a guide to a device you can buy. Some community forks continued afterwards with different names and different menus. The tree here reflects the original releases listed in the picker.

faq.q: How accurate is this reconstruction?
faq.a: The menu titles, their order and their nesting come from the open source interface layer, so the structure is faithful rather than approximate. What cannot be faithful is device state: SIM details, network names and storage figures belong to physical hardware and appear here as sample values marked as such.

faq.q: Why does a phone have browser privacy settings at the top level?
faq.a: Because the whole interface was built from web technologies and the browser engine was the system, not an application on top of it. Controls that other platforms hide inside a browser were phone-wide here, which is one of the more revealing structural differences between this design and its contemporaries.

title: Mac OS 9 Control Panels Simulator - Classic Mac Setup
h1: Open the classic control panels one window at a time
desc: Try the Mac OS 9 control panels in a free browser simulator: 13 panels, 91 rows, only two levels deep, on a classic desktop frame with sample values marked.
lede: Configuration used to mean opening a small window, changing one thing and closing it again. Thirteen panels, ninety-one rows and a maximum depth of two levels is the entire system, which sounds impossibly small until you remember that a computer then did far less. Walking it now is a quick and slightly startling history lesson.
character: Each control panel is a separate item rather than a section of a larger application, and the names tell you exactly which subsystem you are touching. Appearance, Apple Menu Options and General Controls cover how the desktop behaves. Date & Time, Energy Saver, Monitors, Sound, Keyboard and Memory address hardware and housekeeping. File Sharing and TCP/IP handle the network. Startup Disk and Extensions Manager decide what the machine loads when it turns on. There is no unifying window and no search, so the organising principle is simply that you know what the panel is called.

Two levels is the hard ceiling, and it changes the character of everything. A panel either shows you its options immediately or offers a single tabbed screen behind them, so nothing is more than one step from view. Memory and Extensions Manager are the two panels that could break a working machine, and they sit in the same list as the one that controls how fast the cursor blinks, with no warning to separate them. That flatness is why people who learned this system remember panel names rather than paths, and why anyone arriving from a modern settings app finds it disconcerting rather than difficult.
history: Control panels were individual files living in a folder, loaded at startup, which is why each one behaves like a small self-contained program and why the list could grow simply by dropping something new in. Networking, sharing and power management were added this way over successive releases rather than through any redesign. The two versions offered here, 9.2 and 9.0, come from the end of this lineage, shortly before the whole approach was replaced by a single preferences window, so the differences between them are minor.

notable.path: Settings > General Controls > Insertion Point Blinking
notable.why: The rate at which the text cursor blinks was a user setting with its own radio buttons. It is a small thing, but it captures how much of the interface was considered adjustable by ordinary people rather than fixed by the designers.

This changed where the scroll arrows sat and how the scroll bar behaved. Arguments about it were genuinely heated at the time, and it shows how much visual behaviour was exposed before interface designers began locking such choices down.

Sharing a folder meant defining who could reach it, right here on the machine, with no server involved. Seeing the accounts, the owner name and the network toggle in one panel explains how small office networks were actually run.

audience: Anyone maintaining vintage hardware for a museum, a studio or a hobby can plan a setup without waiting for a slow machine to boot. Writers and set designers working on anything period-accurate can check what a panel really contained. Interface students comparing thirteen separate windows with a modern unified settings app get a clean contrast, and people who used these machines can settle an argument about what was where.

faq.q: Are these the real Mac OS 9 control panels?
faq.a: The panel names and their contents follow the shipping system, reconstructed panel by panel because it is not open source. Everything that would describe a particular machine, such as the computer name, the owner name or the current date, appears as a sample value rather than as a claim about any real hardware.

faq.q: What is the difference between 9.2 and 9.0?
faq.a: Very little at the level of the control panel list, which is part of what makes the comparison interesting. Switch between them in the picker to see small additions and wording changes. Sounds and Vibe is blunter still, offering little more than Off, Low, Medium and High.
history: Garmin's watch menus grew outward as the hardware gained sensors. Early models needed little more than activity and display options; optical heart rate, pulse oximetry, sleep staging and stress estimates each brought a new row, and the health entries eventually split into separate categories because one list could no longer hold them. Safety features arrived alongside cellular-connected phones, adding incident detection and contact lists. Payment and connected-service rows followed. title: iOS 6 Settings Simulator: Revisit the 2012 iPhone Menu

title: Windows XP Control Panel Simulator: Explore SP3 Menus

title: Fitbit OS Settings Simulator: Explore Sense Watch Menus
h1: What the Fitbit OS settings look like on a small screen
desc: Browse the Fitbit OS settings menu on a simulated watch face, from Bluetooth and Notifications through to Heart and Health, with all ten top-level entries.
lede: Ten entries, seventy-four rows, and a screen roughly the size of a postage stamp. Watch settings have to be ruthless about what earns a place, and reading the list on a larger display makes the editing choices visible. The simulator draws a watch frame and keeps the menu order intact, so you can scroll a wrist interface with a mouse.
character: The order is a priority list. Bluetooth first, because a watch that is not paired does very little; then Notifications, Display, Exercise and Activity, Heart and Health, Vibration and Audio, Clock Face, Fitbit Wallet, Battery and About. Sensor features and phone features are kept apart, which is unusual. Most wearables mix them together. Here, everything the watch measures about you sits under Heart and Health, and everything the phone pushes at you sits under Notifications. That split makes the menu easy to reason about even when you are tapping with one finger while walking.

Three levels is the limit, and most branches stop at two. Heart and Health is the widest, holding Heart rate, High/low HR alerts, SpO2, Stress management (EDA), Sleep, ECG app and Skin temperature, which is really a list of the sensors the hardware carries. Vibration and Audio takes the opposite approach, offering Normal, Strong, Vibrate on wrist and Chimes and nothing more. Where people get lost is the boundary with the phone app: several things that feel like watch settings are only adjustable on the phone, and the watch menu gives no hint of that.
history: Fitbit's watch software grew out of a fitness tracker interface that had almost no settings at all, and each generation of hardware added a menu entry for the sensor it introduced. That is why Heart and Health reads like a hardware inventory. The two builds listed, OS 5 and OS 4, span the period when the health features were consolidated under a single heading and the clock face and wallet entries settled into their current position. The layout is reconstructed from the shipping interface.

notable.path: Settings > Heart and Health > High/low HR alerts
notable.why: The watch can warn you when resting heart rate sits outside a range you set, which is one of the few settings on the device that people are told about by a clinician rather than discovering for themselves. Finding it takes two taps once you know the branch.

Leaving the screen lit costs battery, and this is the single switch that decides it. It sits with Screen timeout and Screen wake, so the three things that govern when the display is awake stay together rather than scattered, which is worth seeing before you change any of them.

Canned responses to text messages are configured here alongside Calls, Calendar and Do Not Disturb. Knowing the option exists changes how usable the watch feels, because it turns a notification you can only dismiss into one you can answer without reaching for a phone.

audience: Someone comparing wearables before buying wants to know how much can be changed on the wrist rather than in a phone app, and this shows it in a minute. Retail staff demonstrating a watch can rehearse the tour. Carers setting up a device for a relative can find the health alert pages first. Anyone who has lost a watch and is describing its settings to support gets an accurate reference.

faq.q: Is the Fitbit OS menu shown here exact?
faq.a: The structure follows the shipping interface, since this software is not open source and cannot be read from published code. Menu names and their order are reproduced as closely as possible. Everything inside a page that would describe a real device, such as a paired phone name or a battery figure, is a sample value.

faq.q: Which Fitbit OS versions are available?
faq.a: OS 5 and OS 4 are both here, and you can switch between them to see what moved. The differences are mostly about where the health features sit and how the top level is ordered, so a side-by-side look answers most questions about whether an older instruction still applies.

faq.q: Can I change settings on my own watch from here?
faq.a: No. Nothing in the simulator connects to hardware, and no pairing takes place. It is a map of the menu rather than a remote control. Use it to learn where an option lives, then make the change on the watch itself or in the phone app, whichever the setting belongs to.

title: Fire TV Settings Simulator: Browse the Fire OS 8 Menu Tree
h1: Where Fire TV keeps each of its settings pages
desc: Walk the Fire TV settings menu in your browser, from Network and Applications through to Alexa and My Fire TV, arranged as Fire OS presents them on screen.
lede: Eight headings is a short list for a device that streams, plays games, listens for a wake word and runs an app store. The compression shows: several pages carry more than their name suggests. Looking at the tree away from a remote makes it easier to see where Amazon put the things you actually want to change, and where it did not.
character: Network, Display and Sounds, Applications, Controllers and Bluetooth, Alexa, Preferences, Account and Profile and My Fire TV: that is the whole top level. Two things stand out. Alexa gets a heading of its own, which no other television system does, and it holds Alexa Privacy, Hands-Free and Wake Word rather than being folded into a general voice page. My Fire TV, meanwhile, is the engineering drawer, sitting last and unlabelled as such. The naming is plain rather than clever, and each heading is a noun you could say out loud to someone across the room.

Preferences is the page that does the most work and advertises it least. Parental Controls, Privacy Settings, Data Monitoring, Notification Settings, Location and Time Zone all live there, which means privacy, data use and clock settings share a single heading. Display and Sounds goes the other way, offering resolution choices of Auto, 4K (2160p), 1080p and 720p right alongside Match Original Frame Rate, Audio, Display and Screen Saver. Someone hunting for advertising or data controls will usually look under Account and Profile first and find them under Preferences instead.
history: Fire OS is built on Android but replaces the interface above it, and its settings menu has always been organised around the living room rather than the phone. Over successive releases the voice assistant grew from one row into its own top-level heading, and the developer and diagnostic pages were gathered under My Fire TV. The two builds available, Fire OS 8 and Fire OS 7, sit either side of that consolidation. Because the interface layer is not open, the structure here is reconstructed from what the system displays.

notable.path: Settings > Display and Sounds > Match Original Frame Rate
notable.why: Films shot at twenty-four frames a second look wrong when a television forces them to sixty, and this is the switch that stops it. It sits beside the resolution choices rather than under a picture quality heading, which is why so many people never find it.

Streaming quality caps and a running record of how much data each app has used are kept here rather than under Network. If a household is on a metered connection, this page is the one that matters, and it sits two levels from the top.

notable.path: Settings > Applications > Collect App Usage Data
notable.why: Whether the device reports what you watch and for how long is decided under Applications, not under Privacy Settings. Anyone auditing a shared or guest device should check both, because the two pages cover different kinds of collection and neither one mentions the other.

audience: People setting up a television in a rental or a guest room need to know what a previous user could have left switched on, and the tour answers that. Support staff can talk a caller through Preferences without guessing. Anyone comparing streaming boxes before buying can judge how much control each one offers. Parents deciding whether a device suits a child can find the restriction pages before the box arrives.

faq.q: Does this simulator work without a Fire TV?
faq.a: Yes. It runs entirely in the browser with no account and no device involved, so you can explore the menu before buying hardware or after giving it away. Everything shown inside a page, including network names and app lists, is a sample value chosen to make the layout readable.

faq.q: Where are the privacy settings on Fire TV?
faq.a: They are split. Preferences holds Privacy Settings, Data Monitoring and Location, while Applications holds Collect App Usage Data and Alexa holds Alexa Privacy. Walking all three in the simulator is the fastest way to see the full picture, because no single page gathers everything a person would call privacy.

faq.q: Can I compare Fire OS 8 and Fire OS 7?
faq.a: Both versions are available and you can switch between them directly. That makes it straightforward to check whether a page moved between releases, which matters when following older instructions. The comparison mode also lets you set Fire TV beside another television system to see how differently the two organise the same choices.

title: KaiOS Settings Simulator: Explore a Feature Phone Menu
h1: How a KaiOS phone organises its settings without a touchscreen
desc: Explore the KaiOS settings menu in your browser, from Mobile network & Data through to Storage and Device Information, laid out as a feature phone shows it.
lede: Ten headings, no touchscreen, and every choice reachable with a directional pad and a soft key. Designing settings for hardware buttons forces a discipline that touch interfaces lost, and the result is a menu you can navigate without looking. Seeing it on a desktop, where you can read the whole list at once, shows how carefully the ordering was thought through.
character: Airplane Mode sits at position one, above everything else, because on a phone sold for calls and battery life that is the switch people reach for most. Mobile network & Data follows, then Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Display, Sound, Storage, Privacy & Security, Device and Device Information. Radios first, then output, then contents, then the machine itself. It is the same logic a paper manual would use. Nothing is grouped behind an abstraction such as Connections or General, so each heading names exactly one thing and the list stays readable on a very narrow screen.

Depth runs to four levels, which is more than the screen size suggests, and Mobile network & Data is where it goes deepest: Data, Data Roaming, Carrier, APN Settings and Network Type, with configuration pages below them. That is a lot of telecoms vocabulary for a device aimed at people who want a phone that makes calls. Storage tells a similar story, separating Internal, microSD, Manage Storage and Media on SD card because removable cards are still normal here. Someone arriving from a smartphone will find Device and Device Information confusingly similar names.
history: KaiOS descends from the Firefox OS work on a web-based phone platform, and it inherited a settings structure built for browser technology rather than for a native toolkit. That lineage explains headings such as Privacy & Security appearing alongside plainly named hardware pages. The two versions listed, 3.0 and 2.5, span a long gap. The older one shipped on enormous numbers of low-cost handsets, while the newer one modernises the underlying platform and adjusts several settings pages without rebuilding the tree.

notable.path: Settings > Mobile network & Data > APN Settings
notable.why: When a data plan does not work on a new network, this is almost always the page that fixes it, and carrier support scripts point at it constantly. It sits beside Carrier and Network Type, so the three things that decide how the phone connects are together.

notable.path: Settings > Storage > Media on SD card
notable.why: Memory cards remain central on these handsets, and this controls whether photos, music and downloads go to the card or to internal space. It matters more here than on a smartphone, because internal storage is measured in hundreds of megabytes rather than tens of gigabytes.

A larger type size is often the first change anyone makes on a small screen, and it sits with Wallpaper and Screen Timeout rather than under an accessibility heading. Knowing that saves a long hunt for someone setting up the phone on behalf of a relative.

audience: Field workers and travellers who carry a second handset for battery life need to configure it quickly and rarely have a manual. Charities and community projects that distribute low-cost phones can prepare a one-page instruction sheet from the real menu order. Developers building for the platform can check where a permission surfaces. Anyone helping an older relative move to a simpler phone can learn the layout in advance.

faq.q: What kind of phones run KaiOS?
faq.a: Inexpensive handsets with physical keypads, small screens and long battery life, sold in very large numbers in markets where a smartphone is not the default. They run apps and connect to mobile data, but the interface is driven by a directional pad and soft keys rather than by touch, which shapes the whole settings menu.

faq.q: Why is Airplane Mode the first entry?
faq.a: Because it is the switch used most often on a device like this, and putting it first means one press of the down key reaches it. On a keypad phone the cost of an extra step is much higher than on a touchscreen, so frequently used controls climb toward the top of the list.

faq.q: Can I compare KaiOS 3.0 and 2.5?
faq.a: Yes, both are available and switching between them takes one choice. The gap between the two releases is unusually wide, so it is a useful pair to look at when an instruction written for an older handset does not match what is on screen. Sample values fill the pages in both.

title: Windows 98 Control Panel Simulator: Explore 98 SE and 95
h1: Opening the Windows 98 Control Panel one applet at a time
desc: Click through the Windows 98 Control Panel in your browser, from Display and Network to Modems, with the 98 SE and 95 applet layout reconstructed in full.
lede: Every setting on a nineteen-nineties desktop lived inside a small window with tabs along the top, and the whole system amounted to eighty-eight rows. That is fewer choices than a modern phone offers for notifications alone. Working through the applets again is a quick lesson in how much of what a computer now decides for you was once yours to configure.
character: There is no hierarchy at all. Display, Network, System, Add/Remove Programs, Sounds, Mouse, Regional Settings, Date/Time, Passwords, Multimedia and Modems sit as equals in a single folder of icons, and each one opens a dialog with its own tabs. Nothing groups them; alphabetical order is the only organising idea. That flatness means you have to know what an applet is called before you can use it, which is why so much period documentation begins by naming the icon. It also means nothing is ever more than two clicks away.

The depth lives inside the dialogs rather than in the list. Display alone carries Background, Screen Saver, Appearance, Effects and Settings as tabs, with Wallpaper, Pattern, Colors and Screen area beneath them. System splits into General, Device Manager, Hardware Profiles and Performance, and Device Manager was where most troubleshooting ended up. Network exposes Client for Microsoft Networks, Dial-Up Adapter and TCP/IP directly, so configuring a connection meant understanding protocol names. Compared with anything modern, the vocabulary is unapologetically technical and the safety rails are missing.
history: The Control Panel folder arrived with the earliest graphical releases and barely changed shape through the nineteen-nineties; new hardware simply added another icon. Windows 95 established the tabbed dialog style, and Windows 98 Second Edition added applets for the hardware of its day while leaving the arrangement alone. The two builds in the simulator, 98 SE and 95, are close relatives rather than a redesign, so comparing them is mostly a matter of spotting additions. The layout is reconstructed from the shipping interface.

notable.why: Every hardware problem of the era ended here, in a tree of components with warning marks beside the ones that had failed. It sits under System alongside General, Hardware Profiles and Performance, and it is the single page most period support instructions ask you to open.

Screen savers existed to protect phosphor displays from burn-in and became a form of decoration instead. The tab sits beside Background, Appearance, Effects and Settings, and it is worth opening as a reminder that display configuration used to mean choosing patterns and colours by hand.

Optional parts of the operating system were installed and removed here rather than downloaded, which is a genuinely different model. The same applet holds Install/Uninstall and Startup Disk, so adding a component, removing an application and making rescue media all shared one window.

audience: Anyone restoring old hardware or running a period machine for music, games or industrial control needs the applet names right. Teachers illustrating how interface conventions developed can show the tabbed dialog in its original form. Writers and set designers working on anything set in the nineteen-nineties get an accurate reference. People who simply want to see a computer they grew up with can look without finding a working machine.

faq.q: Is this Windows 98 or Windows 95?
faq.a: Both are available and you can switch between them. The two releases share almost all of the Control Panel layout, so the differences are additions rather than rearrangements. Choosing 98 SE gives the later set of applets, while 95 shows the arrangement as it stood when the tabbed dialog style was still new.

faq.q: Does anything here actually run Windows 98?
faq.a: No. This is a reproduction of the settings interface, not an emulator running the operating system, and nothing executes period software. It is useful for finding where an option lived and what it was called. Any figure shown inside a dialog, such as memory or a registered name, is a sample value.

faq.q: Why does the Control Panel have no categories?
faq.a: Grouping came later. In this era each applet was a separate small program dropped into one folder, so the list grew as hardware makers added their own. Category headings only appeared once the number of icons became unmanageable, which is a change you can see by comparing this system with a later release.
